topic.angle: Infinite expected value, small willingness to pay

card.title: The coin game with an infinite average

body.question: A fair coin is flipped until it lands heads. You win $2 if heads comes first, $4 if it comes second, $8 if third, doubling each time. What is the expected payoff?
body.reveal: Infinite. Each possible ending adds $1 on average (half the chance, double the prize, and so on), and the stages never stop. Yet few people would pay even $25 to play. That gap is the St. Petersburg paradox.

probes.question: Why is the St. Petersburg game called a paradox?
options: Its expected payoff is infinite, yet it seems worth very little

probes.question: True or false: the problem was invented by Daniel Bernoulli.

claims.claim: Expected payoff of the game is infinite yet it seems worth very little
claims.quote: the expected payoff of the lottery game is infinite but nevertheless seems to be worth only a very small amount to the participants

claims.claim: Payouts double each stage (2, 4, 8) with probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 per stage
claims.quote: To answer this, one needs to consider what would be the expected payout at each stage

claims.claim: Each stage adds $1 on average and the stages never stop
Few people would pay even $25 to play
claims.quote: Few of us would pay even $25 to enter such a game

claims.claim: Paradox is the gap between willingness to pay and the infinite expected value (probe 1)
claims.quote: The apparent paradox is the discrepancy between what people seem willing to pay to enter the game and the infinite expected value

claims.claim: Problem was invented by Nicolas Bernoulli, not Daniel (probe 2 false)
claims.quote: The problem was invented by Nicolas Bernoulli , who stated it in a letter to Pierre Raymond de Montmort on September 9, 1713
